summary:
Airbus has softened its push to cut remote working after union protests, including repeated strikes at its Spanish sites since July and sporadic protests in France and Britain. The company had planned to require white-collar staff to be on site four days a week by September, up from three, effectively cutting home working to one day. Managers have now been told they can let staff keep existing arrangements averaging two work-from-home days a week, suspending the mandate.

An Airbus spokesperson said the objective is unchanged, citing collective efficiency, knowledge transfer and faster decision-making, but said effective change requires listening to employees, so the transition will be more gradual based on feedback.

The retreat undercuts a campaign led by CEO Guillaume Faury, who told staff in a June memo (first reported by Bloomberg) that home working was a lifeline during COVID-19 when minimising contact was the priority, but that in-person skill sharing is now needed as the industry meets record demand with many new hires. French unions say between a quarter and a third of Airbus staff joined in the past three years, and tens of thousands have left aerospace since COVID-19.

Unions say roughly 40% of Airbus's 14,000 Spanish workers have joined strikes over teleworking, transport, holidays and pay. Production has not been affected, as disruption hit white-collar ancillary functions. Three Spanish unions called a three-hour stoppage to vote on a longer walkout. UGT General Secretary at Airbus Edmundo Otero cited "cautious optimism" on inflation-adjusted pay but wants clarity. Insiders say the intensity of unrest rattled leadership; HR has urged staff to "play together."

Context includes difficulty attracting Gen-Z workers who prioritise work-life balance per Deloitte surveys, competition from higher-paid AI and "digital nomad" sectors noted at Farnborough Airshow, and longstanding Spanish resentment about its role within the group.
